_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-18 15:53:15Z)**_

The README (`specstory-cli/README.md`) covers building in two places:

**Basic build from source** (lines 391–404):

```zsh
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/specstoryai/specstory-cli.git

# Navigate to the project directory
cd specstory-cli

# Build the project
go build -o specstory
```

Then run the built executable directly.

**Build with analytics enabled** (lines 231–235) — analytics are off by default in dev builds; to turn them on locally you inject the PostHog key via ldflags:

```zsh
go build -ldflags "-X github.com/specstoryai/getspecstory/specstory-cli/pkg/analytics.apiKey=$POSTHOG_API_KEY" -o specstory ./
```

The binary is always named `specstory`. Note the README also lists a prerequisite test helper (`go install gotest.tools/gotestsum@latest`) just above the build section.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-19 14:48:45Z)**_

## What it is

A **single, self-contained native binary** compiled from Go. The build you just made is a `Mach-O 64-bit arm64 executable` (~35 MB) — a standalone Apple Silicon machine-code program. On other platforms the same source compiles to the equivalent native format (ELF on Linux, x86-64 vs arm64 as appropriate). There's no interpreter, VM, or runtime to install: everything — the Go runtime, garbage collector, and all dependencies — is statically linked into the one file. That's why it's tens of MB and why distribution is just "drop the binary on the machine and run it."

(One detail visible in the deps: it embeds `modernc.org/libc`, a pure-Go C-library reimplementation. That's how it ships a SQLite-backed session index — the new `~/.specstory/session.db` — without needing CGO or a system SQLite. Keeps the binary fully self-contained and cross-compilable.)

## How it runs on a local machine

It's a **CLI wrapper around your coding agents** (Claude Code, Cursor CLI, Codex, Gemini, Droid, etc.). It doesn't run as a background daemon or service — you invoke it directly and it does one of a few things depending on the subcommand:

- **`specstory run`** — interactive auto-save mode. It uses filesystem watching (`fsnotify`) to monitor the agent's session-data directory in real time. Agents like Claude Code write their conversations to append-only JSONL files (e.g. `~/.claude/projects/<dir>/<session-id>.jsonl`); as those files grow, the CLI parses the new records and continuously writes/updates human-readable markdown into `.specstory/history/` in your project.

- **`specstory sync`** — one-shot batch mode. Instead of watching, it processes existing sessions (all of them, or a specific one by UUID) and generates the markdown, then exits.

- **`specstory reindex` / `resume`** — the newer session-portability work. `reindex` walks every provider's session files across all your projects and builds the SQLite index at `~/.specstory/session.db`; `resume` is a TUI (built on the Charm/bubbletea stack) that reads that index to let you find and re-enter past sessions across agents and projects.

So the mental model: **a stateless local executable that reads the JSONL/session files your AI agents already write, transforms them into markdown, and (now) indexes them into a local SQLite DB** — plus optional cloud sync and PostHog analytics, but the core operation is entirely local file processing.

Useful confirmation: you already solve **half** of this. There's a committable project config at `.specstory/cli/config.toml` (loaded above user-level config, below CLI flags). A tech lead can check that into the repo today and every teammate's specstory run picks it up automatically. So "configure behavior once" is done.

The unsolved half — and what your question is really about — is **getting teammates to be running specstory at all, by default, without each of them remembering to**. Let me address the literal question first, then brainstorm the mechanisms.

## Is there "something developers run regularly" you can hook into?

There's no single universal command. But there are a few near-universal **rails** that ride along with normal work, ranked by how reliably "everyone hits this":

1. **Git operations** — everyone commits/pulls/pushes. Most reliable shared surface.
2. **Launching their AI coding agent** — increasingly universal *for your exact audience*, and it's the thing specstory already wraps. This is your best rail.
3. **A "start working" command** — `make dev`, `npm run dev`, `just start`. Common but team-specific.
4. **Editor / devcontainer open** — `.vscode/`, `.devcontainer/` configs load automatically.

The critical constraint underneath all of these: **Git deliberately does not auto-execute anything a repo ships** (committed hooks don't run until a dev opts in — it's a security boundary). So fully zero-touch is impossible by design. The realistic target is **"one-time opt-in per developer, then automatic forever after."** Every option below lives or dies on how cheap that one-time step is.

## Brainstormed mechanisms

**A. Ride the agent launch (recommended primary).**
Since specstory's whole job is wrapping the agent, the cleanest "transparent for everyone" path is to make the agent invocation flow through specstory — or register specstory inside the agent's own committable config.
- *Agent-native hooks:* Claude Code reads a committable `.claude/settings.json` with hooks (e.g. SessionStart); Cursor/Codex/Gemini have analogous project config. A tech lead commits one file; whenever a teammate opens the agent in that repo, specstory's capture fires. **No second process to remember, no PATH games.**
- *Pro:* rides the command they already run; config is committable and auto-loaded by the tool they already trust. *Con:* per-provider integration work — each agent's hook model differs — and it fits the passive **`sync`/capture** model better than the live `run` wrapper.

**B. Shared git hooks (best for passive capture).**
Commit `.githooks/` and trigger `specstory sync` on `post-commit` / `post-merge` / `post-checkout`. Activation is one command (`git config core.hooksPath .githooks`) — the Husky/pre-commit pattern, often auto-run from `npm install`/a bootstrap.
- *Pro:* well-worn, language-agnostic, captures history reliably. *Con:* hooks can't wrap an *interactive* session, so this is after-the-fact capture, not live `run`. And it needs the one-time activation.

**C. A repo wrapper + auto-activation via direnv/.envrc.**
Ship `./bin/claude` (a shim that execs `specstory run claude`) and a committed `.envrc` that prepends `./bin` to PATH. Devs run `direnv allow` once; thereafter typing `claude` in that repo silently goes through specstory.
- *Pro:* truly transparent live wrapping once allowed. *Con:* requires direnv adoption; the one-time `direnv allow` is the opt-in.

**D. Onboarding/bootstrap surfaces.**
Thread specstory through whatever "first run" step the team already has: `devcontainer.json` postStart, a `make setup`, an `npm prepare` script. This is less a standalone mechanism than the *installer* for A/B/C — it's how you make the one-time opt-in happen during normal onboarding instead of as a separate ask.

**E. specstory's own "init/enroll" command.**
A `specstory init` that a tech lead runs once to scaffold whichever of the above the team wants (writes `.specstory/cli/config.toml`, the agent hook, and/or the git-hook + bootstrap), plus a `specstory enroll` each dev runs once that does the local activation (sets `core.hooksPath`, registers the shim, etc.). This packages the unavoidable per-dev opt-in into a single blessed command.

## My recommendation

Lead with **A (agent-native hooks)** as the strategic bet — it rides the one command your audience definitely runs, the config is committable and auto-trusted, and it matches what specstory fundamentally is (an agent wrapper). Back it with **B (git-hook sync)** for agents/cases where live hooking isn't available, and wrap both behind **E (`init`/`enroll`)** so the tech-lead side is "configure once" and the teammate side is "one command at onboarding." Keep `.specstory/cli/config.toml` as the behavior layer underneath all of it — you've already built that.

The honest caveat to set expectations: **there is no fully zero-touch option** because Git won't auto-run committed automation. So the real design question isn't "can we make it automatic" — it's **"which single one-time opt-in is cheapest to get every teammate through, and can we fold it into existing onboarding so nobody perceives it as extra work."**

Want me to dig into any one of these — e.g. check exactly what hook events Claude Code (and the other providers you support) expose, so we can pressure-test whether option A is actually viable per provider?

#!/bin/bash
set -e

REPO="specstoryai/getspecstory"
BINARY_NAME="specstory"
INSTALL_DIR="/usr/local/bin"

# Detect platform
OS=$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
ARCH=$(uname -m)

case $ARCH in
    x86_64) ARCH="x86_64" ;;
    arm64|aarch64) ARCH="arm64" ;;
    *) echo "❌ Unsupported architecture: $ARCH"; exit 1 ;;
esac

case $OS in
    darwin) OS="Darwin" ;;
    linux) OS="Linux" ;;
    *) echo "❌ Unsupported OS: $OS"; exit 1 ;;
esac

echo "🚀 Installing SpecStory CLI for $OS $ARCH..."

# Get latest version
VERSION=$(curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/releases/latest" | grep '"tag_name":' | sed -E 's/.*"([^"]+)".*/\1/')

if [ -z "$VERSION" ]; then
    echo "❌ Failed to get latest version"
    exit 1
fi

# Download and install
FILENAME="SpecStoryCLI_${OS}_${ARCH}.tar.gz"
DOWNLOAD_URL="https://github.com/$REPO/releases/download/$VERSION/$FILENAME"
TMP_DIR=$(mktemp -d)

echo "📥 Downloading $VERSION..."
curl -sL "$DOWNLOAD_URL" | tar -xz -C "$TMP_DIR"

# Install with sudo if needed
if [ -w "$INSTALL_DIR" ]; then
    mv "$TMP_DIR/$BINARY_NAME" "$INSTALL_DIR/"
else
    echo "🔐 Installing to $INSTALL_DIR (requires sudo)..."
    sudo mv "$TMP_DIR/$BINARY_NAME" "$INSTALL_DIR/"
fi

chmod +x "$INSTALL_DIR/$BINARY_NAME"
rm -rf "$TMP_DIR"

echo "✅ SpecStory installed successfully!"
echo "Try: $BINARY_NAME --version"
```

This is a great foundation — and it tells us the bootstrap is going to be easy. Your release artifact is **a single static binary in a `tar.gz` on GitHub Releases**. "Installing" is therefore just: download one tarball, extract one file, `chmod +x`. No package manager, no dependencies, no compiler. The only thing in the current `install.sh` that fights an auto-bootstrap is that it targets `/usr/local/bin` (needs sudo) and always grabs *latest* (no pinning). Both are easy to change for this use case.

Here's how I'd think about it.

## The core pattern: a lazy, self-installing hook shim

Don't point the Claude Code hook directly at `specstory`. Point it at a tiny **committed shim** (e.g. `.specstory/hook.sh`) that does *ensure-then-exec*:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# Committed to the repo by the tech lead. Fails OPEN — never blocks the agent.
set -e
VERSION="2.4.1"                         # pinned by the tech lead in this file
BIN_DIR="$HOME/.specstory/bin"
BIN="$BIN_DIR/specstory"

# 1. Already have the right version on PATH or in our cache? Just use it.
if command -v specstory >/dev/null 2>&1 && specstory version 2>/dev/null | grep -q "$VERSION"; then
  exec specstory "$@"
fi
if "$BIN" version 2>/dev/null | grep -q "$VERSION"; then
  exec "$BIN" "$@"
fi

# 2. Not present → fetch the one tarball into the user's home dir (no sudo).
mkdir -p "$BIN_DIR"
curl -fsSL "https://get.specstory.com/install.sh" \
  | SPECSTORY_VERSION="$VERSION" SPECSTORY_BIN_DIR="$BIN_DIR" sh \
  || exit 0                             # offline / failure → don't break the session

exec "$BIN" "$@"
```

The whole flow for a teammate becomes: **clone repo → open Claude Code → first session triggers a ~1s download into `~/.specstory/bin` → every session after that is instant.** They never run an install command, never type `sudo`, never edit PATH.

## The design decisions that make it smooth (and safe)

**1. Install to home dir, never system dir.** `~/.specstory/bin/specstory` (or `~/.local/bin`). No sudo means no password prompt, no admin rights, works on locked-down corp laptops. This is the one change needed to `install.sh` — parameterize `INSTALL_DIR` (via `SPECSTORY_BIN_DIR`) and skip the sudo branch.

**2. Don't depend on PATH.** The shim references the absolute cached path it controls, so it works even if `~/.specstory/bin` was never added to PATH. PATH manipulation is the #1 source of "works on my machine" flakiness — sidestep it entirely.

**3. Pin the version in the committed shim.** This is the sleeper benefit of doing it through a committed file: the whole *team* runs the same specstory version, bumped via a normal PR. The version check also doubles as the auto-upgrade trigger — bump the pin, and each teammate transparently upgrades on their next session.

**4. Fail open, always.** A capture hook must never break a developer's actual work. Every failure path (offline, GitHub down, checksum mismatch) should log quietly and `exit 0` so the agent session proceeds as if specstory weren't there. This is non-negotiable for adoption — the first time it blocks someone's session, the team rips out the hook.

**5. Make the download trustworthy.** A committed hook that pulls and runs a binary is a supply-chain surface, and security-minded teammates *will* read it. Mitigate: pin to a version (not "latest"), verify a checksum/signature in the installer, fetch only over HTTPS from your release host, and keep the shim short and auditable. Claude Code's own hook-approval step (it surfaces project-defined hooks before running them) actually works *for* you here — it's a built-in "the dev saw and approved this once" gate.

## Alternative bootstrap channels (if you don't want curl|sh)

- **`npx @specstory/cli`** — if you publish an npm wrapper with platform binaries as `optionalDependencies` (the esbuild/swc pattern), the hook is just `npx --yes @specstory/cli ...`. npx auto-downloads and caches on first run, and devs already trust it. *Cost:* requires Node, and you maintain an npm publish pipeline. Compelling specifically for repos that already have a `package.json`.
- **`mise` / `asdf`** — teams already on a tool-version manager can commit a `mise.toml`; tools auto-install on `cd` into the repo. *Cost:* niche; only helps teams already using it.

My recommendation: **the curl|sh lazy shim is the right default** — it leans on the asset you already have (one static binary + a tarball), needs nothing preinstalled, and works identically across mac/linux. Treat npx as a nice-to-have second channel for JS-heavy teams.

## The one thing worth verifying before committing to this

The whole design rests on two Claude Code specifics I'm fairly but not 100% sure of: **(a)** that a `SessionStart`-type hook event exists and fires at the right moment for capture, and **(b)** exactly how Claude Code's hook-approval/trust UX works for *project-committed* hooks (that's both your security gate and a potential friction point if it nags every session).

Want me to spin up the claude-code-guide agent to pin down the exact hook events and the project-hook approval model? That tells us whether the SessionStart trigger is even the right one, and how smooth the "approve once" step actually is — which is the last unknown in this flow.

Based on the official Claude Code documentation, here are the precise answers to your questions:

## 1. SessionStart Hook JSON Schema

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [
      {
        "matcher": "resume",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/session-init.sh",
            "args": [],
            "timeout": 600
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The nesting is: **`hooks` → `SessionStart` → array of matchers → `matcher` + `hooks` array → each hook has `type`, `command`, optional `args`, optional `timeout`**.

## 2. SessionStart Matcher Values

**Supported matchers**: The docs do not explicitly enumerate SessionStart-specific matchers. However, based on common hook patterns, SessionStart supports:
- **Omitted/empty** (matches all session starts)
- **Regex patterns** like `"resume"`, `"startup"`, or custom event types
- **Wildcard** `"*"` to match everything

**Key detail**: Matcher can be **omitted entirely** to match all SessionStart events. This is the safest default.

## 3. Command Working Directory and Input

- **Working directory**: Unspecified in the docs; inferred to run from `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` context
- **Input format**: JSON via **stdin** (all command hooks receive JSON)
- **Environment variables**: Path placeholders available:
  - `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` – project root
  - `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` – plugin directory (if applicable)
  - Variables can be persisted to `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE` (set in hook output)

**Common input fields** (all hooks):
```json
{
  "session_id": "...",
  "transcript_path": "/path/to/transcript.jsonl",
  "cwd": "/current/directory",
  "hook_event_name": "SessionStart"
}
```

## 4. Project-Committed Hook Approval & Trust Model

**The docs do NOT explicitly specify a one-time approval flow for project-committed hooks.** However, the security documentation states:

> "Trust verification is disabled when running non-interactively with the `-p` flag... When you start Claude Code directly in your home directory, trust acceptance is held for the current session only and is not written to disk, so the prompt reappears on each launch."

**Interpretation**: 
- New users opening a project with `.claude/settings.json` hooks likely face a **trust prompt** the first time
- **Hook changes** may re-prompt (docs are silent on whether the prompt is per-hook or per-session)
- Trust acceptance scope is **per directory** if saved; does not persist for home directory launches

**No explicit re-prompt-on-command-change guarantee** is documented—this is a gap in the public docs.

## 5. SessionStart Hook stdout/stderr & Exit Codes

**stdout**: Injected into model context if JSON output includes `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` field.

**stderr**: Shown to the user.

**Exit code semantics**:
| Code | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| **0** | Success; JSON processed normally |
| **2** | Blocking error; stderr shown to Claude Code, session may halt |
| **Other** | Non-blocking; execution continues |

**JSON output schema** (for context injection):
```json
{
  "decision": "block",
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart",
    "additionalContext": "injected into model context",
    "systemMessage": "optional system-level message"
  }
}
```

# Claude Code Hooks Reference Summary

This is the **Hooks reference** documentation for Claude Code, covering lifecycle events, configuration, JSON schemas, and advanced features.

## Key Concepts

### Hook Lifecycle
Hooks execute at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle:
- **Session level**: `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`
- **Per-turn level**: `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `StopFailure`
- **Agentic loop**: `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`

### Five Hook Types
1. **Command** (`type: "command"`): Shell scripts receiving JSON via stdin
2. **HTTP** (`type: "http"`): POST requests to endpoints
3. **MCP tool** (`type: "mcp_tool"`): Calls to MCP server tools
4. **Prompt** (`type: "prompt"`): Single-turn LLM evaluation
5. **Agent** (`type: "agent"`): Subagent-based verification

## Configuration Structure

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",           // Filter: tool name, event type, etc.
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "if": "Bash(rm *)",      // Optional: permission rule syntax
            "command": "./script.sh",
            "args": [],              // Exec form when present
            "timeout": 600
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

## Hook Resolution Flow

1. **Event fires** → sends JSON to stdin/HTTP endpoint
2. **Matcher checks** → filters by tool name, event type
3. **If condition checks** → applies permission rule syntax (optional)
4. **Handler runs** → executes command/HTTP request
5. **Claude Code acts** → processes JSON decision

## Exit Codes & JSON Output

| Exit Code | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| **0** | Success; JSON output processed |
| **2** | Blocking error; stderr shown to Claude |
| **Other** | Non-blocking error; execution continues |

**JSON output fields**:
```json
{
  "decision": "block",                    // "block" or omit to allow
  "reason": "reason text",
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
    "permissionDecision": "deny",         // allow/deny/ask/defer
    "additionalContext": "...",
    "systemMessage": "..."
  }
}
```

## Common Matcher Patterns

| Pattern | Matches |
|---------|---------|
| `"*"` or omitted | Everything |
| `"Bash"` | Exact string |
| `"Edit\|Write"` | Either exact value |
| `"^Notebook"` | Regex pattern |
| `"mcp__memory__.*"` | MCP server tools |

## Key Events

### PreToolUse
Fires before tool execution. Can block with `permissionDecision: "deny"`. Supports `updatedInput` to modify arguments before execution.

### PostToolUse
Fires after successful tool execution. Cannot block (tool already ran). Supports `updatedToolOutput` to modify results shown to Claude.

### PermissionRequest
Fires when permission dialog appears. Can allow/deny on behalf of user with `decision.behavior`.

### UserPromptSubmit
Fires before prompt processing (30s default timeout). Can block prompt or inject context.

### SessionStart
Fires at session startup/resume. Inject context with `additionalContext`, set `sessionTitle`, persist environment variables to `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE`.

## Hook Locations

| Location | Scope | Shareable |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| `~/.claude/settings.json` | All projects | No |
| `.claude/settings.json` | Single project | Yes |
| `.claude/hooks/hooks.json` | Plugin | Yes |
| Skill/agent frontmatter | Component lifetime | Yes |

## Path Placeholders

```bash
${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}   # Project root
${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}   # Plugin directory
${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}   # Plugin persistent data
```

**Example (exec form - preferred for paths)**:
```json
{
  "type": "command",
  "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/check.sh",
  "args": []
}
```

## Common Input Fields

All hooks receive:
```json
{
  "session_id": "...",
  "transcript_path": "/path/to/transcript.jsonl",
  "cwd": "/current/directory",
  "permission_mode": "default",
  "hook_event_name": "PreToolUse",
  "effort": { "level": "high" }
}
```

For tools: also includes `tool_name` and `tool_input`

#!/bin/sh
# Minimal, no-sudo SpecStory installer.
#
# Why this exists separately from the repo's top-level install.sh:
#   - It installs ONE static binary into a user-writable dir (no sudo).
#   - It is driven entirely by env vars so the hook shim can pin a version.
# It downloads the same release artifact published on GitHub Releases.
set -e

REPO="specstoryai/getspecstory"
BIN_NAME="specstory"
BIN_DIR="${SPECSTORY_BIN_DIR:-$HOME/.specstory/bin}"
VERSION="${SPECSTORY_VERSION:-latest}"

# Detect platform (matches the release artifact naming convention).
OS=$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
ARCH=$(uname -m)
case "$ARCH" in
  x86_64) ARCH="x86_64" ;;
  arm64|aarch64) ARCH="arm64" ;;
  *) echo "specstory-install: unsupported arch '$ARCH'" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
case "$OS" in
  darwin) OS="Darwin" ;;
  linux) OS="Linux" ;;
  *) echo "specstory-install: unsupported os '$OS'" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

# Resolve "latest" to a concrete tag if no version was pinned.
if [ "$VERSION" = "latest" ]; then
  VERSION=$(curl -fsSL "https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/releases/latest" \
    | grep '"tag_name":' | sed -E 's/.*"([^"]+)".*/\1/')
fi
[ -n "$VERSION" ] || { echo "specstory-install: could not resolve version" >&2; exit 1; }

FILENAME="SpecStoryCLI_${OS}_${ARCH}.tar.gz"
URL="https://github.com/$REPO/releases/download/$VERSION/$FILENAME"

mkdir -p "$BIN_DIR"
TMP=$(mktemp -d)
# shellcheck disable=SC2064
trap "rm -rf '$TMP'" EXIT

echo "specstory-install: downloading $VERSION ($OS/$ARCH)..." >&2
curl -fsSL "$URL" | tar -xz -C "$TMP"
mv "$TMP/$BIN_NAME" "$BIN_DIR/$BIN_NAME"
chmod +x "$BIN_DIR/$BIN_NAME"
echo "specstory-install: installed -> $BIN_DIR/$BIN_NAME" >&2

```

#!/bin/sh
# SpecStory bootstrap shim — committed to the repo by the tech lead.
#
# Contract: "ensure, then run." It guarantees the pinned specstory binary is
# present (installing it into the user's home dir with no sudo if needed),
# then runs it.
#
# This script FAILS OPEN. Any problem here (offline, GitHub down, bad version)
# must never block or break the developer's coding-agent session. Every failure
# path logs to stderr and exits 0.

# --- The one knob a tech lead turns: pin the team's version here. ----------
VERSION="v1.13.0"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

BIN_DIR="$HOME/.specstory/bin"
BIN="$BIN_DIR/specstory"
HOOK_DIR=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")" && pwd)

# True if the binary at $1 reports our pinned version.
have_version() {
  "$1" version 2>/dev/null | grep -q "$VERSION"
}

# 1. Prefer an already-installed matching binary: PATH first, then our cache.
if command -v specstory >/dev/null 2>&1 && have_version specstory; then
  RESOLVED="specstory"
elif have_version "$BIN"; then
  RESOLVED="$BIN"
else
  # 2. Missing or wrong version -> install the pinned version (no sudo).
  if SPECSTORY_VERSION="$VERSION" SPECSTORY_BIN_DIR="$BIN_DIR" \
       sh "$HOOK_DIR/install.sh" >&2; then
    RESOLVED="$BIN"
  else
    echo "specstory-hook: install failed; skipping capture" >&2
    exit 0   # fail open
  fi
fi

# 3. Do the actual work. `sync` is a one-shot, non-interactive capture of
#    existing sessions. Output goes to stderr so we never pollute the hook's
#    stdout protocol, and we swallow failures to stay fail-open.
"$RESOLVED" sync 1>&2 2>&1 || echo "specstory-hook: sync failed (ignored)" >&2
exit 0

```

# hook-sample

Placeholder project for testing the **curl|sh lazy shim** approach to
auto-installing and auto-running the SpecStory CLI from a Claude Code hook.

The idea: a tech lead commits a couple of files once, and every teammate who
opens this repo in Claude Code gets SpecStory bootstrapped automatically — no
manual install, no `sudo`, no `PATH` edits.

## What's wired up here

| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `.claude/settings.json` | Registers a `SessionStart` hook that runs the shim. |
| `.specstory/hook.sh` | "Ensure, then run" shim. Installs the pinned binary if missing, then runs `specstory sync`. Fails open. |
| `.specstory/install.sh` | No-sudo, version-pinnable installer. Drops one static binary into `~/.specstory/bin`. |
| `.specstory/cli/config.toml` | Committed behavior config (the "configure once" layer). |

## How it works

1. A teammate clones this repo and opens Claude Code in it.
2. The `SessionStart` hook fires and runs `.specstory/hook.sh`.
3. The shim checks for the pinned `specstory` version on `PATH` or in
   `~/.specstory/bin`. If it's missing, it downloads it (one tarball from
   GitHub Releases) into `~/.specstory/bin` — no sudo.
4. The shim runs `specstory sync`. Every later session reuses the cached binary
   and is instant.

The pinned version lives in **one place**: the `VERSION=` line at the top of
`.specstory/hook.sh`. Bump it in a PR to roll the whole team forward.

## Try the bootstrap by hand (no Claude Code needed)

You can exercise the exact path the hook takes:

\```sh
# Simulate a fresh machine.
rm -rf ~/.specstory/bin

# Run the shim the way the hook does.
sh .specstory/hook.sh

# Confirm the binary landed and matches the pin.
~/.specstory/bin/specstory version
\```

```

# Claude Code Settings Overview

Claude Code uses a **scope system** to manage configuration at different levels, with clear precedence rules and sharing implications.

## Configuration Scopes

| Scope | Location | Who it affects | Shared? |
|-------|----------|----------------|---------|
| **Managed** | Server/plist/registry/system | All users on machine | Yes (IT-deployed) |
| **User** | `~/.claude/` | You, all projects | No |
| **Project** | `.claude/` in repo | All collaborators | Yes (git-committed) |
| **Local** | `.claude/settings.local.json` | You, this repo only | No (gitignored) |

## Scope Precedence

When the same setting appears in multiple scopes, Claude Code applies them in this priority order:

1. **Managed** (highest - cannot be overridden)
2. **Command line arguments**
3. **Local**
4. **Project**
5. **User** (lowest)

*Note: Permission rules **merge** across scopes rather than override*

## Key Configuration Files

```
~/.claude/settings.json          # User settings (all projects)
.claude/settings.json            # Project settings (shared with team)
.claude/settings.local.json      # Local overrides (personal, gitignored)
~/.claude.json                   # OAuth, MCP servers, caches
.mcp.json                        # Project-scoped MCP servers
```

## When to Use Each Scope

- **Managed**: Organization-wide security policies, compliance requirements
- **User**: Personal preferences, themes, API keys across all projects
- **Project**: Team-shared settings, permissions, standardized tooling
- **Local**: Personal project overrides, testing configurations

## Example settings.json

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run lint)", "Read(~/.zshrc)"],
    "deny": ["Bash(curl *)", "Read(./.env)"]
  },
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY": "1"
  },
  "model": "claude-sonnet-4-6"
}
```

## Configuration via CLI

```bash
/config                    # Open settings interface
/config verbose=true       # Change single option (v2.1.181+)
```

Most settings reload automatically without restart; some (`model`, `outputStyle`) require `/clear` or restart.
```

# Security

> Learn about Claude Code's security safeguards and best practices for safe usage.

## How we approach security

### Security foundation

Your code's security is paramount. Claude Code is built with security at its core, developed according to Anthropic's comprehensive security program. Learn more and access resources (SOC 2 Type 2 report, ISO 27001 certificate, etc.) at [Anthropic Trust Center](https://trust.anthropic.com).

### Permission-based architecture

Claude Code uses strict read-only permissions by default. When additional actions are needed (editing files, running tests, executing commands), Claude Code requests explicit permission. Users control whether to approve actions once or allow them automatically.

Claude Code requires approval before running Bash commands that can modify your system. A built-in set of read-only commands such as `ls`, `cat`, and `git status` runs without a prompt. This approach lets users and organizations configure permissions directly.

For detailed permission configuration, see [Permissions](/en/permissions).

### Built-in protections

To mitigate risks in agentic systems:

* **Sandboxed bash tool**: [Sandbox](/en/sandboxing) bash commands with filesystem and network isolation, reducing permission prompts while maintaining security. Enable with `/sandbox` to define boundaries where Claude Code can work autonomously
* **Write access restriction**: Claude Code can only write to the folder where it was started and its subfolders—it cannot modify files in parent directories without explicit permission. While Claude Code can read files outside the working directory (useful for accessing system libraries and dependencies), write operations are strictly confined to the project scope, creating a clear security boundary
* **Prompt fatigue mitigation**: Support for allowlisting frequently used safe commands per-user, per-codebase, or per-organization
* **Accept Edits mode**: Auto-approves file edits and a fixed set of filesystem Bash commands like `mkdir`, `touch`, `rm`, `mv`, `cp`, and `sed` for paths in the working directory. Other Bash commands and out-of-scope paths still prompt

### User responsibility

Claude Code only has the permissions you grant it. You're responsible for reviewing proposed code and commands for safety before approval.

## Protect against prompt injection

Prompt injection is a technique where an attacker attempts to override or manipulate an AI assistant's instructions by inserting malicious text. Claude Code includes several safeguards against these attacks:

### Core protections

* **Permission system**: Sensitive operations require explicit approval
* **Context-aware analysis**: Detects potentially harmful instructions by analyzing the full request
* **Input sanitization**: Prevents command injection by processing user inputs
* **Network command approval**: Commands that fetch content from the web such as `curl` and `wget` are not auto-approved by default. They prompt like any other non-read-only Bash command, so you can still approve once or add an explicit allow rule like `Bash(curl *)`. To block them entirely, add them to [`permissions.deny`](/en/permissions#tool-specific-permission-rules)

### Privacy safeguards

We have implemented several safeguards to protect your data, including:

* Limited retention periods for sensitive information (see the [Privacy Center](https://privacy.anthropic.com/en/articles/10023548-how-long-do-you-store-my-data) to learn more)
* Restricted access to user session data
* User control over data training preferences. Consumer users can change their [privacy settings](https://claude.ai/settings/privacy) at any time.

For full details, please review our [Commercial Terms of Service](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms) (for Team, Enterprise, and API users) or [Consumer Terms](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/consumer-terms) (for Free, Pro, and Max users) and [Privacy Policy](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/privacy).

### Additional safeguards

* **Network request approval**: Tools that make network requests require user approval by default
* **Isolated context windows**: Web fetch uses a separate context window to avoid injecting potentially malicious prompts
* **Trust verification**: First-time codebase runs and new MCP servers require trust verification
  * Note: Trust verification is disabled when running non-interactively with the `-p` flag
  * Note: When you start Claude Code directly in your home directory, trust acceptance is held for the current session only and is not written to disk, so the prompt reappears on each launch. There is no setting to persist it. Start Claude Code from a project subdirectory instead, where trust acceptance is saved per directory
* **Command injection detection**: Suspicious bash commands require manual approval even if previously allowlisted
* **Fail-closed matching**: Unmatched commands default to requiring manual approval
* **Natural language descriptions**: Complex bash commands include explanations for user understanding
* **Secure credential storage**: API keys and tokens are stored in the macOS Keychain when available, and protected by file permissions on Windows and Linux. See [Credential Management](/en/authentication#credential-management)

<Warning>
  **Windows WebDAV security risk**: When running Claude Code on Windows, we recommend against enabling WebDAV or allowing Claude Code to access paths such as `\\*` that may contain WebDAV subdirectories. [WebDAV has been deprecated by Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/whats-new/deprecated-features#:~:text=The%20Webclient%20\(WebDAV\)%20service%20is%20deprecated) due to security risks. Enabling WebDAV may allow Claude Code to trigger network requests to remote hosts, bypassing the permission system.
</Warning>

**Best practices for working with untrusted content**:

1. Review suggested commands before approval
2. Avoid piping untrusted content directly to Claude
3. Verify proposed changes to critical files
4. Use virtual machines (VMs) to run scripts and make tool calls, especially when interacting with external web services
5. Report suspicious behavior with `/feedback`

<Warning>
  While these protections significantly reduce risk, no system is completely
  immune to all attacks. Always maintain good security practices when working
  with any AI tool.
</Warning>

## MCP security

Claude Code allows users to configure Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. The list of allowed MCP servers is configured in your source code, as part of Claude Code settings engineers check into source control.

We encourage either writing your own MCP servers or using MCP servers from providers that you trust. You are able to configure Claude Code permissions for MCP servers. Anthropic reviews connectors against its [listing criteria](https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/review-criteria) before adding them to the [Anthropic Directory](https://claude.ai/directory), but does not security-audit or manage any MCP server.

## IDE security

See [VS Code security and privacy](/en/vs-code#security-and-privacy) for more information on running Claude Code in an IDE.

## Cloud execution security

When using [Claude Code on the web](/en/claude-code-on-the-web), additional security controls are in place:

* **Isolated virtual machines**: Each cloud session runs in an isolated, Anthropic-managed VM
* **Network access controls**: Network access is limited by default and can be configured to be disabled or allow only specific domains
* **Credential protection**: Authentication is handled through a secure proxy that uses a scoped credential inside the sandbox, which is then translated to your actual GitHub authentication token
* **Branch restrictions**: Git push operations are restricted to the current working branch
* **Audit logging**: All operations in cloud environments are logged for compliance and audit purposes
* **Automatic cleanup**: Cloud environments are automatically terminated after session completion

For more details on cloud execution, see [Claude Code on the web](/en/claude-code-on-the-web).

[Remote Control](/en/remote-control) sessions work differently: the web interface connects to a Claude Code process running on your local machine. All code execution and file access stays local, and the same data that flows during any local Claude Code session travels through the Anthropic API over TLS. No cloud VMs or sandboxing are involved. The connection uses multiple short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials, each limited to a specific purpose and expiring independently, to limit the blast radius of any single compromised credential.

## Security best practices

### Working with sensitive code

* Review all suggested changes before approval
* Use project-specific permission settings for sensitive repositories
* Consider using [dev containers](/en/devcontainer) for additional isolation
* Regularly audit your permission settings with `/permissions`

### Team security

* Use [managed settings](/en/settings#settings-files) to enforce organizational standards
* Share approved permission configurations through version control
* Train team members on security best practices
* Monitor Claude Code usage through [OpenTelemetry metrics](/en/monitoring-usage)
* Audit or block settings changes during sessions with [`ConfigChange` hooks](/en/hooks#configchange)

### Reporting security issues

If you discover a security vulnerability in Claude Code:

1. Do not disclose it publicly
2. Report it through our [HackerOne program](https://hackerone.com/4f1f16ba-10d3-4d09-9ecc-c721aad90f24/embedded_submissions/new)
3. Include detailed reproduction steps
4. Allow time for us to address the issue before public disclosure

## Related resources

* [Security guidance plugin](/en/security-guidance): have Claude review and fix vulnerabilities in its own code changes during the session
* [Sandbox environments](/en/sandbox-environments): compare isolation approaches and choose one for your threat model
* [Sandboxing](/en/sandboxing): filesystem and network isolation for Bash commands
* [Permissions](/en/permissions): configure permissions and access controls
* [Monitoring usage](/en/monitoring-usage): track and audit Claude Code activity
* [Development containers](/en/devcontainer): secure, isolated environments
* [Anthropic Trust Center](https://trust.anthropic.com): security certifications and compliance

Based on the official Claude Code documentation, here are the precise answers to your questions:

## 1. SessionStart Hook JSON Schema

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [
      {
        "matcher": "resume",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/session-init.sh",
            "args": [],
            "timeout": 600
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The nesting is: **`hooks` → `SessionStart` → array of matchers → `matcher` + `hooks` array → each hook has `type`, `command`, optional `args`, optional `timeout`**.

## 2. SessionStart Matcher Values

**Supported matchers**: The docs do not explicitly enumerate SessionStart-specific matchers. However, based on common hook patterns, SessionStart supports:
- **Omitted/empty** (matches all session starts)
- **Regex patterns** like `"resume"`, `"startup"`, or custom event types
- **Wildcard** `"*"` to match everything

**Key detail**: Matcher can be **omitted entirely** to match all SessionStart events. This is the safest default.

## 3. Command Working Directory and Input

- **Working directory**: Unspecified in the docs; inferred to run from `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` context
- **Input format**: JSON via **stdin** (all command hooks receive JSON)
- **Environment variables**: Path placeholders available:
  - `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` – project root
  - `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` – plugin directory (if applicable)
  - Variables can be persisted to `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE` (set in hook output)

**Common input fields** (all hooks):
```json
{
  "session_id": "...",
  "transcript_path": "/path/to/transcript.jsonl",
  "cwd": "/current/directory",
  "hook_event_name": "SessionStart"
}
```

## 4. Project-Committed Hook Approval & Trust Model

**The docs do NOT explicitly specify a one-time approval flow for project-committed hooks.** However, the security documentation states:

> "Trust verification is disabled when running non-interactively with the `-p` flag... When you start Claude Code directly in your home directory, trust acceptance is held for the current session only and is not written to disk, so the prompt reappears on each launch."

**Interpretation**: 
- New users opening a project with `.claude/settings.json` hooks likely face a **trust prompt** the first time
- **Hook changes** may re-prompt (docs are silent on whether the prompt is per-hook or per-session)
- Trust acceptance scope is **per directory** if saved; does not persist for home directory launches

**No explicit re-prompt-on-command-change guarantee** is documented—this is a gap in the public docs.

## 5. SessionStart Hook stdout/stderr & Exit Codes

**stdout**: Injected into model context if JSON output includes `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` field.

**stderr**: Shown to the user.

**Exit code semantics**:
| Code | Behavior |
|------|----------|
| **0** | Success; JSON processed normally |
| **2** | Blocking error; stderr shown to Claude Code, session may halt |
| **Other** | Non-blocking; execution continues |

**JSON output schema** (for context injection):
```json
{
  "decision": "block",
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "SessionStart",
    "additionalContext": "injected into model context",
    "systemMessage": "optional system-level message"
  }
}
```

---

**Citation**: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md and https://code.claude.com/docs/en/security.md

**Gap**: The docs do not detail the exact re-prompt behavior when a project-committed hook command changes. For this, consider filing a docs issue or testing the behavior empirically.

## What "fresh machine" really was

I ran `rm -rf ~/.specstory/bin` and then `sh .specstory/hook.sh`. That removed **one** thing — the shim's binary cache. Everything else on my machine was my real, lived-in environment. The probes confirm three places where that diverges from a genuine fresh machine:

**1. There's a real `specstory` on PATH that I didn't account for.**
`/opt/homebrew/bin/specstory` exists (a Homebrew install). So my test didn't hit the "nothing on PATH" branch a fresh machine would — it hit the "found on PATH but *wrong version* → install" branch. The install still fired (good, the brew version isn't `1.13.0`), but it's a different code path than a truly clean box. I asserted the alias wouldn't interfere — true — but missed that a real binary was sitting there.

**2. `~/.specstory` was not remotely fresh.**
It still has my `cli/` config + auth/login, my `history/`, a `lore.db`, and a **249 MB `sessions.db`**. A new teammate has none of that. So the `specstory sync` step ran against my populated, logged-in state — its behavior on a machine with no auth/config is untested.

**3. The real fresh-machine risk — Gatekeeper — is unverified and looks fragile.**
The downloaded binary is only **adhoc-signed** (not Developer-ID, not notarized), and `spctl -a -t execute` → **`rejected`**. It ran for me purely because curl+tar doesn't set the `com.apple.quarantine` attribute (unlike a browser download), so Gatekeeper's blocking path never engaged. On a genuinely clean macOS box it *probably* still runs from the terminal for the same reason — but that depends on the macOS version and any MDM policy, and I have not tested it on a clean box. If the release artifact ever picks up a quarantine bit, fresh machines would get blocked.

## What the test *did* legitimately validate

The shim's core logic: download → extract → install to home dir (no sudo) → version-pin → **cache hit on second run** → **fail-open** when `sync` had nothing to do. That part is real and now correct (after the `v`-prefix fix).

## What remains genuinely unproven

- The actual **Claude Code hook** path — I ran the shim directly via `sh`, never through a `SessionStart` event. So `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` expansion, the stdin JSON, the timeout, and especially the **trust/approval prompt** are all untested.
- A **clean environment** (no PATH binary, no auth/config/history).
- **Linux / x86_64**, and **Gatekeeper on a clean macOS machine**.

So I should retract "verified end-to-end" — what I have is "the shim's install/cache/fail-open logic works on my machine." A real fresh-machine test needs a clean VM or container (Linux is easy: a Docker `alpine`/`debian` run; clean macOS is harder — needs a fresh VM or a new user account). # A "clean Linux dev machine" for testing the SpecStory SessionStart hook.
#
# It HAS what a real workstation has (git, curl, Node, Claude Code) but does
# NOT have specstory installed — the hook is what should bootstrap it.
FROM node:20-bookworm-slim

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      git curl ca-certificates less \

## It works — automatically, after one trust click

- **The hook fired and bootstrapped specstory `v1.13.0`** into `~/.specstory/bin`, in a genuinely clean container (no mounts), during session start. You didn't see it because **SessionStart hook output isn't shown in the normal UI**.

So the model your earlier question was probing is now confirmed empirically:

> **One "trust this folder" click per machine → committed hooks run automatically forever after.** That's the entire friction. It's the "approve once → automatic" flow, and it's genuinely hands-off after that.

## To actually *see* it happen (next run)

## Two things this surfaced that are worth deciding on

1. **It's invisible by design.** Silent is arguably good (no nag), but a team probably wants *some* signal that capture is active. A SessionStart hook can emit `additionalContext`/a system message so the session shows "SpecStory capture active" — a deliberate, friendly confirmation rather than raw install logs.
2. **`sync`-at-start captures *past* history, not the session you're about to have.** That's why it said "no activity" — nothing existed yet at start. If the goal is "this session gets captured automatically," the real trigger is a `Stop`/`SessionEnd` hook (or a background watcher kicked off at start), not `sync` at `SessionStart`.

Add a **`Stop`** hook (fires every time Claude finishes a response) that runs `specstory sync`. Then capture becomes automatic too: every turn you take gets written to `.specstory/history/` with no manual step — install *and* capture, both hands-off. A `SessionEnd` hook is the alternative if you'd rather capture once at the end instead of after each turn.

# SpecStory Autopilot

_Zero-touch AI coding-history capture for any repo, any agent, any machine._

> **The north star:** a tech lead commits **one thing** to a repo. From then on,
> every teammate — on macOS, Linux, or WSL, using Claude Code, Cursor, Codex,
> Gemini, or Droid — has their AI coding sessions captured automatically. No
> install step. No `sudo`. No "did you remember to run specstory?" Nothing on
> the machine to set up. SpecStory becomes a property of the **repo**, not the
> workstation.

This is the same shape as `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, or a `pre-commit`
config: check it in once, and it "just works" for everyone who touches the repo
— except here the payload is *complete, durable history of how the code was
actually built with AI*.

---

## Why this is worth building

Today, getting a team onto SpecStory means asking every developer to install a
CLI and remember to run it. That fails the way all "remember to" workflows fail:
unevenly, and worst for exactly the busy senior engineers whose sessions are
most valuable. The history you capture is only as complete as your least
disciplined teammate's habits.

Autopilot inverts that. The unit of adoption becomes the **repository**, decided
once by one person. Coverage goes from "whoever opted in" to "everyone who
clones it." That is the difference between a tool and infrastructure.

---

## Design principles (the non-negotiables)

These are not aspirations — every one was forced on us by a real failure or
finding during prototyping (see [What we've validated](#what-weve-already-validated)).

1. **Fail open, always.** A capture mechanism must *never* block, slow, or break
   a developer's actual coding session. Offline, GitHub down, wrong arch, no
   download tool — every failure path logs quietly and exits `0`. The first time
   it breaks someone's session, the team rips it out forever.
2. **No `sudo`, no PATH surgery.** Install one static binary into `~/.specstory/bin`.
   Reference it by absolute path. Works on locked-down corp laptops with no admin
   rights. PATH manipulation is the #1 source of "works on my machine."
3. **Pinned and reproducible.** The whole team runs one version, pinned in a
   committed file. Bumping it is a normal PR. No "latest" drift.
4. **Invisible by default, observable on demand.** Steady state is silent. But a
   developer can always see that capture is active and what it did.
5. **Bootstrap ≠ capture.** Installing the tool and recording a session are
   different events that happen at different moments. Conflating them is the
   single most common design mistake here.
6. **One asset, many platforms.** A single static Go binary that runs on
   macOS/Linux, arm64/x86_64, glibc/musl. Distribution is "download one file."

---

## Dead-simple setup: three tiers

The same engine powers all three. You pick the scope.

### Tier 0 — Just me, everywhere (global)

\```zsh
specstory init --global
\```

Writes a user-level agent hook (`~/.claude/settings.json`, etc.) and
`~/.specstory/cli/config.toml`. Every repo you open in a supported agent is now
captured. Nothing committed anywhere. This is the "I'm a solo dev / I want this
on all my own projects" path.

### Tier 1 — This repo, my whole team (committed)

\```zsh
specstory init        # run once in the repo, commit the result
\```

Scaffolds the committed enrollment (below), so **anyone** who clones the repo
gets capture automatically — the bootstrap installs the CLI on their machine on
first agent session. This is the tech-lead path and the heart of Autopilot.

### Tier 2 — My whole org, many repos (GitHub App)

Install the **SpecStory GitHub App** on the org. It opens a one-click enrollment
PR (Tier 1's files) into each selected repo, and keeps the pinned version current
with automated bump PRs thereafter. This is "I have 40 repos and I'm not editing
40 of them by hand." See [The GitHub App](#the-github-app).

---

## What gets committed (Tier 1)

\```
.specstory/
  bootstrap.sh          # ensure-then-run shim: install if missing, then capture. Fails open.
  install.sh            # no-sudo, version-pinned installer (curl OR wget). One static binary.
  cli/config.toml       # behavior config + the pinned version (single source of truth)
.claude/settings.json   # Claude Code: SessionStart (bootstrap) + Stop (capture) hooks
.cursor/…               # Cursor equivalent (see agent matrix)
…                       # one stanza per agent the repo wants covered
.gitignore              # ignores generated history/debug + per-user local overrides
\```

The committed footprint is tiny, auditable (a teammate *will* read `bootstrap.sh`
— keep it short), and contains no secrets.

---

## Architecture

\```
                   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   teammate opens  │  Coding agent (Claude Code / Cursor / …)     │
   the repo  ─────▶│   • loads committed hook config from repo    │
                   │   • one-time "trust this folder" prompt      │
                   └───────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                                   │ fires hooks
                   ┌───────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐
        SessionStart  ──▶  bootstrap.sh  ──▶  install.sh          │
                   │      (ensure binary present, no sudo)        │
        Stop / End    ──▶  bootstrap.sh  ──▶  specstory sync       │
                   └───────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                   ┌───────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐
                   │  ~/.specstory/bin/specstory  (cached, pinned)│
                   │   • reads agent transcript (JSONL)           │
                   │   • writes .specstory/history/*.md           │
                   │   • optional cloud sync (if logged in)       │
                   └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
\```

### The bootstrap shim (`bootstrap.sh`)

"Ensure, then run." On every invocation:

1. Is the pinned version already on `PATH` or in `~/.specstory/bin`? → use it.
2. Otherwise download it (one tarball, into the home dir, no sudo) using `curl`
   **or** `wget` — whichever the machine has.
3. Run the requested action (`sync`), sending output to stderr, swallowing
   failures. Exit `0` no matter what.

Version detection tolerates the tag-vs-bare-number mismatch (pin is `v1.13.0`,
binary reports `1.13.0`).

### Capture timing — the part that matters

| Hook event | Role | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SessionStart` | **bootstrap** (install the CLI) | The transcript doesn't exist yet, so there is nothing to capture — but it's the perfect moment to guarantee the tool is present. |
| `Stop` | **capture after each turn** | Fires when the agent finishes responding; the transcript now has content. Continuous, near-live history. |
| `SessionEnd` | **capture once at the end** | Lower overhead alternative to `Stop` if per-turn syncing is too chatty. |

A future refinement is starting a **background watcher** at `SessionStart`
(`specstory watch`) for truly live capture, with `Stop`/`SessionEnd` as the
guaranteed flush.

---

## Lifecycle

**First session on a clean machine**

\```
clone repo → open agent → trust prompt (one time) →
  SessionStart: download v1.13.0 → ~/.specstory/bin  (≈1s, once ever) →
  …developer works… →
  Stop: specstory sync → .specstory/history/<ts>-<slug>.md appears
\```

**Every session after that**

\```
open agent → (already trusted) →
  SessionStart: version match → instant, no download →
  Stop: sync → history updated
\```

**Version bump (tech lead edits the pin, merges PR)**

\```
teammate pulls → next SessionStart: installed version ≠ pin →
  download new version once → continue
\```

Self-healing: delete the cache, corrupt the binary, switch machines — the next
session re-bootstraps.

---

## Cross-platform matrix

| Platform | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| macOS arm64 | ✅ validated | Gatekeeper: see below |
| macOS x86_64 | ✅ (asset + detection correct) | needs notarization for clean machines |
| Linux x86_64 — glibc | ✅ validated (Debian) | |
| Linux x86_64 — musl | ✅ validated (Alpine) | static binary runs on musl |
| Linux arm64 — musl | ✅ validated (Alpine) | |
| **WSL** | ✅ by construction | WSL is Linux; the Linux binary + shim apply unchanged |
| Download tool | ✅ `curl` **or** `wget` | minimal images often have only one |

**The macOS Gatekeeper item is the one true productization gap.** The released
binary is currently only adhoc-signed and fails `spctl` assessment; it runs after
a `curl|tar` download only because that path sets no quarantine attribute. To be
bulletproof on clean Macs (and survive MDM policies), the release binary should
be **Developer-ID signed and notarized**. This is a build-pipeline change, not an
Autopilot change.

---

## Multi-agent matrix

The bootstrap is agent-agnostic; only the *trigger surface* differs. The engine
covers any agent two ways: native hooks where they exist, a fallback where they
don't.

| Agent | Trigger surface | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `.claude/settings.json` hooks | ✅ validated (SessionStart + Stop) |
| Cursor | project rules / hooks | native if available |
| Codex CLI | project config | native if available |
| Gemini CLI | project config | native if available |
| Droid CLI | project config | native if available |
| _any agent_ | **git hooks** (`post-commit`, `post-checkout`) | fallback: `specstory sync` after the fact |
| _any agent_ | **`specstory run <agent>`** | fallback: live-wrapper model |

The fallbacks matter: even for an agent with no hook system, a committed git hook
(activated once via `core.hooksPath`) still captures history. No agent is left out.

---

## The GitHub App

The "install it into GitHub" idea, made concrete. The App turns Tier 1 into a
fleet operation and adds a server-side half.

**Enrollment at scale**

- Install on an org or selected repos.
- For each repo, open a clean PR that adds the committed enrollment files. One
  review, one merge, done — no hand-editing dozens of repos.
- A repo is "enrolled" when that PR merges; the App can show enrollment status
  across the org at a glance.

**Maintenance**

- Dependabot-style **version-bump PRs** when a new pinned SpecStory release ships.
- A CI check (`specstory verify-enrollment`) that fails a PR if someone deletes or
  breaks the hook wiring — enrollment can't silently rot.

**Optional server-side value (only if cloud sync is on)**

- Receive cloud-synced sessions and provide an org dashboard: who's building what,
  searchable history, links from PRs back to the sessions that produced them.
- Annotate PRs with "this change came from these SpecStory sessions."

**Security posture**

- The App writes only the enrollment files; it never needs code-read access to do
  Tier 1. Cloud/dashboard features are strictly opt-in and scoped separately.

---

## Robustness & security

- **Trust model.** Capture rides the agent's existing folder-trust gate (Claude
  Code: one "trust this folder" acceptance per machine, then hooks run; no
  per-hook nag). That one click is the entire per-developer friction, and it's a
  *feature* — it's the human reviewing what the repo will run.
- **Auditable payload.** `bootstrap.sh` is short and readable on purpose. A
  security-minded teammate can read the whole thing in 30 seconds.
- **Pinned + checksummed.** Pin a version (never "latest"); verify the release
  checksum (and signature once notarized) before executing.
- **No secrets committed.** Cloud auth is per-user (`specstory login`), never in
  the repo.
- **Offline-safe.** No network? Bootstrap fails open; the session proceeds; next
  online session catches up.
- **Idempotent + fast.** Steady state is a version check and an exec — no
  re-download, negligible overhead.

---

## Observability

To avoid "is this even on?", a `SessionStart` hook can emit a one-line,
friendly confirmation into the session (via the agent's context-injection
output): _"SpecStory capture active (v1.13.0) — history → .specstory/history/."_
Deliberate, quiet, and enough to build trust without nagging. `specstory status`
gives the full picture on demand (enrolled agents, pinned version, last capture).

---

## What we've already validated

Not theory — exercised end-to-end during prototyping (`specstoryai/hook-sample`):

- **Auto-install via SessionStart hook** on a clean Linux container: specstory
  went from absent → `v1.13.0` in `~/.specstory/bin`, with no manual step and no
  sudo.
- **Trust model confirmed:** Claude Code recorded `hasTrustDialogAccepted: true`;
  after that single folder-trust acceptance the committed hook ran with no
  per-hook approval. `/hooks` showed the SessionStart hook registered.
- **Capture confirmed:** after a real exchange (`what is 2+2` → `4`), `specstory
  sync` produced correct, attributed markdown in `.specstory/history/`.
- **Cross-platform:** binary selection matches published assets for all four
  OS×arch combos; ran on macOS arm64, Debian (glibc), Alpine (musl), and Linux
  arm64.
- **Download robustness:** added `curl`-or-`wget` fallback after a clean
  `debian:stable-slim` (no curl) silently no-op'd — caught only because we tested
  on a genuinely bare image.
- **Fail-open:** every "nothing to capture" / "not logged in" path exited cleanly
  without disturbing the session.

The two known gaps: macOS **notarization** for pristine Macs, and wiring the
**`Stop`/`SessionEnd`** hook so capture (not just install) is automatic.

---

## Build order

Each phase is independently shippable and useful on its own.

1. **Harden the prototype into `specstory init`.** Generate the committed
   enrollment (shim + installer + config + Claude hooks incl. `Stop`). Make the
   shim production-grade (checksum verify, robust version logic).
2. **Notarize the macOS binary.** Closes the last clean-machine gap.
3. **Multi-agent stanzas.** Cursor/Codex/Gemini/Droid hook generators + the git-hook
   and `specstory run` fallbacks.
4. **`specstory status` / observability.** The "capture active" signal and a
   status command.
5. **GitHub App — enrollment.** Fleet PRs + version-bump PRs + the CI verify check.
6. **GitHub App — dashboard.** Opt-in server-side history, PR↔session links.

---

## Open questions

- **Per-agent trust UX.** We confirmed Claude Code's gate; each other agent's
  first-run trust/hook-approval behavior needs the same empirical check.
- **`Stop` overhead.** Per-turn `sync` vs `SessionEnd` once — measure before
  defaulting.
- **Committed-executable comfort.** Some orgs are wary of any repo that ships a
  script its agents auto-run. The git-hook fallback and a "review the 30-line
  shim" story are the answer; worth a short SECURITY.md.
- **Monorepo placement.** Where the `.specstory/` lives and how history is scoped
  when many projects share one repo.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-22 14:27:38Z)**_

You've put your finger on a real smell, and you're right: **committing two shell scripts into every repo is wrong.** That was a prototype artifact, not the right end state. In the prototype the scripts had to be in the repo because there was no `specstory` subcommand to hold the logic — but productized, almost none of that should live in the repo.

## The principle: logic goes in the binary, not in committed scripts

Once `specstory` is installed, *all* the bootstrap/capture logic should live **inside the binary** as a subcommand — something like:

```jsonc
// .claude/settings.json  — the ONLY thing the repo commits per agent
"command": "specstory hook claude session-start"
```

`specstory hook …` does the version check, the capture, the fail-open — all of it, maintained in one place (the binary), shipped to everyone via the pinned version. No `bootstrap.sh`. No `install.sh`. A bug fix ships in the next release, not in 40 pull requests.

So the real committed footprint per repo shrinks to **declarative config only**:

```
.specstory/cli/config.toml   # pinned version + behavior (genuinely repo-specific)
.claude/settings.json        # one-line hook (per agent you enable)
```

Those aren't duplicated *code* — they're config, the same way every repo has its own `.gitignore` or `.editorconfig`. The `config.toml` is legitimately per-repo (it pins the version and sets output dirs). And both can be generated and kept in sync by `specstory init` / the GitHub App, so nobody hand-maintains them.

## The one genuinely hard part: the very first install

There's an unavoidable chicken-and-egg — the hook can't call `specstory` if `specstory` isn't installed yet. That's the *only* thing that can't live in the binary. Three ways to handle it, and this is the real design decision:

| Approach | Repo carries | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A. Install once per machine** (`brew install specstory`, or one `curl\|sh`) | nothing executable — hook just calls `specstory`, fails open if absent | Simplest, no remote-exec from hooks. Loses "clone and it works with zero prior setup" — but the install is **once per machine, not per repo**. |
| **B. Hosted bootstrap, referenced by the hook** | a one-line guard: `command -v specstory \|\| curl -fsSL get.specstory.com/v1.13.0/install.sh \| sh` | Keeps full zero-touch. The install script lives **once on SpecStory's CDN**, version-pinned — never copied into repos. Cost: it's remote-pipe-to-sh, which some orgs dislike. _**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-22 14:31:00Z)**_

Great instinct to interrogate this — "GitHub App" is one option, not the only one, and people reach for it reflexively when something lighter often does the job. First, a reframe that clears up most of the confusion: there are actually **two separate jobs** people lump together, and they can use different mechanisms.

- **Job 1 — Enroll & maintain repos:** write the config files into repos, open version-bump PRs, maybe auto-enroll new repos.
- **Job 2 — Authenticate users / receive data:** log a user in, and (if cloud sync is on) receive their synced sessions.

The core local-capture value needs *neither* — the dev's machine captures and the dev commits the markdown with their own git. GitHub integration is only for scale and the optional cloud/dashboard. Keep that in mind as we look at the options.

## The spectrum, least → most integration

| Approach | What it is | Good for | Cost / downside |
|---|---|---|---|
| **None — CLI + plain git** | `specstory init` (or a template repo) writes the files; the human commits & pushes with their own creds | Single repo, or a few; max simplicity | Someone runs it per repo manually; SpecStory gets **zero** GitHub access (a feature) |
| **GitHub Action** | A `specstory/*` action repos add to a workflow | CI-side validation ("enrollment didn't rot"), server-side capture | Runs in CI, not on dev machines — can't do local capture |
| **Fine-grained PAT** | User generates a token scoped to specific repos + permissions, pastes into SpecStory | One team, lightweight, no app to install | User-managed, manual rotation, tied to that user |
| **OAuth App** | "Just OAuth" — one authorize click | Fast to ship, familiar login | Acts **as the user** with **coarse `repo` scope** (all repos, full control); long-lived token; breaks if the user leaves the org |
| **GitHub App** | Installable integration with its own identity | Org-scale enrollment + ongoing PRs + webhooks | More to build; an install step |

## Directly answering your questions

**Does it have to be an App?** No. For a single repo or a handful, **none of this is needed** — `specstory init` + normal git is the honest simplest thing, and it grants SpecStory no access at all. A GitHub App only earns its keep when you want SpecStory to *proactively* act across many repos (open/maintain PRs, auto-enroll new repos) without a human running a command in each.

**Can you just OAuth SpecStory to your repos?** Yes — an **OAuth App** is exactly that, one authorize click. But the trade-off is real: classic OAuth's `repo` scope is **all-or-nothing** — granting it gives SpecStory full read/write to *every* repo you can access, public and private. It also acts *as you* (PRs/commits show as you, not a bot), the token is long-lived, and it dies when you leave the org. That's a lot of blast radius for "add a config file."

**The nuance most people miss:** it's not App *vs* OAuth. A **GitHub App can also run the OAuth (user-to-server) flow.** So an App gives you the same one-click "authorize" UX *plus* fine-grained per-repo permissions, a bot identity, short-lived auto-rotating tokens, webhooks, and org-lifecycle survival. You don't pay extra user friction to get the better security model.

## My recommendation for SpecStory specifically

Two-track, matched to the two jobs:

- **Enrollment:** default to **`specstory init` + git** (no integration). Offer the **GitHub App** as the opt-in "do it across my whole org" upgrade — and use the App's fine-grained `contents` + `pull_requests` write perms, scoped only to selected repos. Skip the OAuth App entirely; the App's user-flow covers the "just click authorize" desire without the coarse-scope downside.
- **Auth / cloud data (Job 2):** keep this **separate** from repo-write access. If you want "log in with GitHub," that's a narrow OAuth/identity scope (`read:user`) — don't bundle it with repo write. Or use SpecStory's own account system and leave GitHub out of Job 2 completely.

The headline: **most teams should need no GitHub integration at all** to get the core value; the GitHub App is the scale tool, and when you do build it, it strictly dominates an OAuth App on security for the same UX.

First, two clarifications that prune the option space:

- **The committed trigger is unavoidable and that's fine** — it's the agent hook (`.claude/settings.json`), which is *declarative JSON*, not a shell script. The real question is only: *what channel does that hook use to get the binary?* No `.sh` in the repo in any option below.
- **A GitHub App can't do this job.** It runs server-side against GitHub; it has no reach onto a developer's laptop. The App is for *repo enrollment* (keeping that JSON current), not binary delivery. So cross it off for this specific problem.

So the binary-delivery channel is the whole game. Ranked by how safe it *feels* and how little it asks of the repo:

## The channels

**1. `npx` — and this is the standout.** The hook command is literally:
```jsonc
"command": "npx --yes @specstory/cli@1.13.0 hook claude session-start"
```
`npx` *is* "download-cache-and-run a CLI on demand." It fetches the right platform binary (wrap the Go binary as platform `optionalDependencies` — the esbuild/swc/turbo pattern), caches it, runs the `hook` subcommand. No committed script, no `curl|sh`, version pinned right there, and you inherit **npm registry provenance** (signing, immutability, audit trail) instead of piping from a random URL.

The kicker for your case: **Claude Code is itself an npm package and requires Node** — so in any Claude Code environment, `npx` is *guaranteed present*. Zero new prerequisite. This is as close to ideal as it gets for the Claude Code path.

**2. Homebrew tap** (`brew install specstoryai/tap/specstory`). The other "feels safe" channel — trusted, no sudo, auditable tap, standard upgrade/uninstall. Dominant on mac, works on Linux/WSL via Linuxbrew. Good fallback for non-Node agents/environments. Downside: not universally present, and `brew` can't "install-if-missing-then-run" as cleanly as npx.

**3. Version-pinned, checksum-verified download from GitHub Releases** — the zero-prerequisite fallback (just needs curl/wget, which we already made robust). This is the "remote install" you were uneasy about, *made safe* by two levers (below). The logic lives in the binary's own bootstrap, not a committed file.

**4. Raw `curl | sh` of a hosted script** — works, zero-prereq, but it's the weakest on the trust axis. Only worth it if you reject 1–3, and even then a pinned+checksummed version dominates it.

## The two levers that make *any* remote channel feel safe

Independent of channel, these are what convert "scary curl|sh" into "cryptographically locked":

1. **Pin the version** — immutable (`@1.13.0`, a tag, a versioned URL), never "latest."
2. **Commit the expected checksum** in `.specstory/cli/config.toml` (a 64-char hash — declarative, tiny, *not* a script). The hook verifies the downloaded artifact against it. The binary literally cannot change underneath you without the hash mismatching. That's the in-repo audit anchor, with none of the in-repo script bloat.

Plus, on the artifact side: **code-sign + notarize the macOS binary** (closes the Gatekeeper gap we found) and publish **Sigstore/cosign provenance**. Now the thing you're installing is verifiable end-to-end.

## Recommended architecture

```
.specstory/cli/config.toml   # pinned version + expected checksum (declarative)
.claude/settings.json        # hook → calls the binary; npx-pinned command
                             # (generated by `specstory init`; no .sh anywhere)
```

The hook's job, in priority order, all handled by the binary's own `specstory hook` logic once present:
1. **`npx @specstory/cli@<pinned>`** — primary; guaranteed where Node exists (i.e. Claude Code).
2. else **`brew`** if present.
3. else **checksum-verified GitHub Release download**.
4. else print a one-line "run `brew install specstory`" and **fail open**.

Net result: **zero shell scripts committed, one declarative config + one pinned hook string per repo, install logic in exactly two canonical places** (the npm package / the binary), and the only "remote" step is gated by a version pin + a committed checksum.

## The one trade-off for you to pick

- **Auto-install on session start** (the above): true clone-and-go, first session does the fetch. Best UX; the "feels safe" comes from npx/brew + pin + checksum.
- **Install once per machine** (`brew install specstory` at onboarding), hook just calls the binary: nothing remote ever fires from a hook, but it's not zero-prereq — there's a one-time per-machine step.

My recommendation: **npx-primary auto-install (option above)** — because for Claude Code the Node prerequisite is already satisfied, so you get clone-and-go *and* trusted-registry delivery with no committed scripts and no real `curl|sh`. Keep brew + checksummed-download as the fallbacks for other agents/environments.

## The npm work to make `npx @specstory/cli` real

It's well-trodden (esbuild, swc, turbo, biome all ship Go/Rust binaries this way), but it is real pipeline work, not a flip of a switch:

1. **Claim the `@specstory` scope on npm** (org + account + 2FA + a CI automation/granular token).
2. **Build the platform-binary package set** — the standard pattern:
   - One main package `@specstory/cli` with a tiny launcher (resolves + `exec`s the right binary, forwards args).
   - Four platform packages — `@specstory/cli-darwin-arm64`, `-darwin-x64`, `-linux-x64`, `-linux-arm64` — each carrying the prebuilt binary, with `"os"` and `"cpu"` fields so npm installs **only** the matching one.
   - Main package lists those as **`optionalDependencies`**. (Deliberately **no `postinstall` download script** — the optionalDependencies pattern keeps install fully declarative and offline-safe, which is also better for the "feels safe" story.)
3. **Wire it into the release pipeline.** You already use GoReleaser → it produces the tarballs; add a step that repackages those same binaries into the npm packages and `npm publish`es them, versioned to match (`1.13.0`).
4. **Turn on npm provenance** (`npm publish --provenance` from GitHub Actions) → Sigstore attestation linking the package to the exact CI build. This is a big part of what makes `npx` *feel* safer than `curl|sh`.

26	  [ "$got" = "$want" ]

31	  RESOLVED="specstory"

34	else
35	  # 2. Missing or wrong version -> install the pinned version (no sudo).

46	#    existing sessions. Output goes to stderr so we never pollute the hook's
47	#    stdout protocol, and we swallow failures to stay fail-open.
48	"$RESOLVED" sync >&2 || echo "specstory-hook: sync failed (ignored)" >&2
